sections.heading: AFFILIATIONS
ABSTRACT
sections.text:
Herein, a piezoelectric vibration energy harvester (PVEH) using liquid as an energy-capturing medium is proposed to simultaneously achieve ultralow frequency, low intensity, and multidirectional vibration energy harvesting in a horizontal plane, which is difficult to realize using traditional PVEHs. The proposed harvester comprises a cylindrical container with a certain liquid, a piezoelectric cantilever beam, ropes, and floater-lever arrays. The experimental results indicate that the proposed harvester with a single floater-lever can generate $9 . 8 \mu \mathrm { W }$ under an ultralow frequency $( 2 . 6 \ \mathrm { \ H z } )$ ) and a low intensity vibration excitation $( 0 . 0 3 \mathrm { g } )$ , and the normalized power density is $8 . 8 9 \mu \mathrm { W } / ( \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } \mathrm { ~ g } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { ~ H z ) }$ . Under a multidirectional vibration excitation $3 6 0 ^ { \circ }$ in the horizontal plane) with frequencies below $3 \ \mathrm { ~ H z }$ and an acceleration of $0 . 0 3 { \mathrm { g } } ,$ the two proposed harvesters with three and four floater-levers indicate a maximum output powerp $\left( \mathrm { { P } _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } } \right)$ deviation of $2 4 . 9 2 \%$ and $2 8 . 3 1 \%$ , respectively, and an angle bandwidth of $3 6 0 ^ { \circ }$ (using $\sqrt { 2 } / 2 \mathrm { P } _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ as the standard). All the experimental results indicate that the proposed PVEH is highly promising as an energy supply of wireless sensor networks distributed in ultralow frequency, low intensity, and multidirectional applications. Published under license by AIP Publishing. https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0022881 Piezoelectric vibration energy harvesters (PVEHs) have continuously garnered the interest of researchers and are highlighted as one of the most promising solutions for replacing chemical batteries to power sensors in wireless sensor networks (WSNs) owing to their high-power density and simple structures.1–6 A PVEH is typically composed of a piezoelectric cantilever beam and a proof mass attached to the free end of the cantilever. Owing to its structural characteristics, PVEHs can only perform well when vibration excitation is operated at a high operation frequency in the direction parallel to the thickness of the beam. However, the easily available vibration sources in ambient environments typically exhibit ultralow frequency $( < 5 \mathrm { { H z } ) ^ { 7 } }$ and multidirectional characteristics such as human motion,8–10 wave motion,11 and moving vehicles,12 which significantly reduce the efficiency of typical PVEHs. Therefore, PVEHs that can operate effectively in an ultralow frequency and a multidirectional vibration environment are necessitated for WSNs in the Internet of Things. In terms of low-frequency vibration energy harvesting, a direct method is to reduce the spring stiffness of the cantilever beam, e.g., by adopting a curved beam13–15 or using polymeric substrates.16,17 Moreover, an effective method is to introduce a frequency upconversion mechanism in which a low-frequency structure is used to harvest low-frequency vibration energy, followed by pushing a high-frequency piezoelectric cantilever beam to oscillate through a contact18–21 or non-contact force,22–26 thereby achieving a high mechanical–electrical conversion. In multidirectional vibration energy harvesting, a typical method is to increase the number of piezoelectric cantilever beams that vibrate in a single direction and then distribute them in different operational directions.28–31 Another method is based on a threedimensional flexible material structure to harvest multidirectional vibration.32,33 However, few studies have reported energy harvesting in ultralow frequencies and multidirectional vibrations. For example, $\mathrm { X u }$ et $a l . ^ { 3 4 }$ presented a piezoelectric cantilever with a pendulum instead of a fixed proof mass to achieve ultralow frequency and multidirectional vibration energy harvesting. Furthermore, Wu et al.7 proposed a modified pendulum-structure PVEH that had a spring integrated piezoelectric element instead of a piezoelectric cantilever beam, which evened out the strain over the piezoelectric elements and enhanced the energy harvesting performance. Nonetheless, a large space was required for the swing of the pendulum structure because the ultralow frequency characteristics were achieved by increasing the length of the pendulum structure, which is inconvenient for practical applications. Hence, PVEHs with favorable performances in ultralow frequency and multidirectional environments are urgently required. ![](images/60e58c1ffae3440f465dce60365b41cff307f65c4e7f4943a5520da40d4310a1.jpg) G. 1. (a) Components of the proposed PVEH; (b) operating principle; and (c) real-time output voltage of the piezoelectric cantilever In fact, liquid is a substance with favorable ultralow frequency and multidirectional shaking characteristics35 owing to its lower force between molecules, better diffusion fluidity, and shape conformance to a container. Additionally, a liquid can shake easily under a low vibration intensity, thereby reducing the potential barrier height of the PVEH.36 In other words, a PVEH adopting liquid as an energy-capturing medium can operate effectively in an ultralow frequency, low intensity, and multidirectional vibration environment. ![](images/5b8f1655ac56f1586a8c58a69b329d347d9b592a7bcca4d6b7b89f160c5e473c.jpg) FIG. 2. Hence, we herein propose a PVEH using liquid (water) as an energy-capturing medium to simultaneously achieve ultralow frequency, low intensity, and multidirectional vibration energy harvesting. As shown in Fig. 1(a), the proposed PVEH is mainly composed of a cylindrical container with a certain amount of water, a piezoelectric cantilever beam, and an array of floater-levers. The floater-lever arrays were fixed in the container by a shaft on the supporter, and the ends of the floater-lever arrays were vertically connected to the end of the piezoelectric cantilever beam by nylon ropes. The two ends of the rope were tied with small holes at the ends of the floater-lever and the piezoelectric cantilever beam. When a horizontal excitation was applied to the container, owing to the liquid sloshing and the limitations of the shaft, one or more floater-levers began to swing around the shaft and then deformed the piezoelectric cantilever beam through the rope connection; hence, an electrical output can be produced based on the piezoelectric effect. To elucidate the operating principle of the proposed PVEH, a PVEH with a single floater-lever can be used as an example because of its structural symmetry. As demonstrated in Fig. 1(b), when the cylindrical container is excited by external vibration, the liquid will slosh and drive the floater-lever to swing up and down. During the upward swing of the floater-lever, the cantilever beam bent downward under the traction of the floater-lever. During the downward swing of the floater-lever, because the resonance frequency of the cantilever was much greater than the swing frequency of the floater-lever, the piezoelectric cantilever beam and the floater-lever rebound to a certain distance until the rope relaxed, and the piezoelectric cantilever beam began to oscillate. For a more comprehensive understanding of the operating principle of the proposed PVEH, the real-time output voltage of the piezoelectric cantilever beam is shown in Fig. $1 ( \mathrm { c } )$ , where the shaded areas in the three colors correspond to stages 2, 3, and $^ { 4 , }$ as shown in Fig. 1(b). Initially, a prototype of the PVEH was fabricated, and a measurement system was established to test the performance, as shown in Fig. 2. Both the cylindrical container and floater-levers were fabricated via 3D printing using an ultraviolet curable resin as the material (SOMOS Imagine 8000, Royal DSM Group, Netherlands). In addition, the inside of the floater-levers was printed to be hollow such that they can float on the liquid surface. The structure of the floater-lever was designed as a fan shape to adapt to the curved edge of the cylindrical container, and the bottom of the floater was designed as a trianglebaffle structure to achieve an efficient energy transmission.37 More detailed parameters are shown in Fig. 2(a). The piezoelectric cantilever beam (PZT 5J, S118-J1SS-1808YB) was produced by the Mide Technology Company in the USA, and the detailed parameters are listed in Table I. Finally, the fabricated PVEH was fixed at a shaker through an L-shaped fixture, where the shaker was used as a horizontal vibration source. A signal generator through a power amplifier was used to drive the shaker oscillated at a specified frequency and amplitude. The real vibration intensity was monitored using an accelerator and recorded by a data acquisition (DAQ) system through a charge amplifier. Furthermore, the DAQ system was used to record the output voltage of the resistance load, which was a resistance box connected to the PVEH. ![](images/30630ab2bcec5acfb3973c5dbe8c2c6a0c84faeae0f32780fe931cf385808910.jpg) FIG. 3. (a) The amplitude-frequency characteristic of the RMS value of the open-circuit voltage of the PVEH with a single floater-lever; and (b) resonance frequency of the liquid sloshing as a function of container radius $( R )$ and liquid height $( H )$ . ![](images/35ef88d74c3e7e644bd70c5b89672b8d982fa5ebe3639c134b116cbcb97e6dee.jpg) FIG. 4. Output power of the PVEH with the single floater-lever: (a) as a function of frequency at different accelerations; and (b) as a function of external load resistant at a frequency of $2 . 6 \mathsf { H z }$ and an acceleration of $0 . 0 3 \mathfrak { g }$ . In the experiments, we first studied the ultralow frequency characteristic of the proposed PVEH with a single floater-lever structure at a liquid height of $2 0 \mathrm { m m }$ . Figure 3(a) shows the root mean square (RMS) value of the open-circuit voltage $( V _ { R M S } )$ of the PVEH at an acceleration of $0 . 0 3 { \mathrm { g } }$ . As is shown, the output response of the proposed PVEH exhibited resonance characteristics similar to those of the traditional PVEH. This is attributed to the natural vibration characteristic of liquid sloshing in a cylindrical container, and the first mode resonance frequency of the liquid sloshing without a floater-lever structure can be calculated as follows:3 5 $$ f = \frac { 1 } { 2 \pi } \sqrt { \frac { g \lambda } { R } } \operatorname { t a n h } \left( \frac { \lambda H } { R } \right) , $$ where $\lambda$ corresponds to the first-order sloshing mode damping ratio coefficient of the liquid, which is generally 1.841; $^ { \mathrm { g } }$ is the acceleration of gravity, which is equal to $9 . 8 ~ \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ ; $R$ is the radius of the cylindrical container; and $H$ is the height of the liquid. The resonance frequency of the liquid sloshing was calculated to be $2 . 4 \mathrm { H z } ,$ whereas the measured resonant frequency of the liquid was $2 . 6 \mathrm { H z }$ . The resonant frequency difference was attributed to the effect of the floater-lever, rope, and piezoelectric cantilever beam on the sloshing of the liquid under excitation, and it was more evident when the size of the floater-lever increased, as shown in the multidirectional energy harvesting later. For practical applications, the resonant frequency must correspond to the environments for resonanttype PVEHs. When the excitation frequency changes, the tunability of the resonant frequency of the proposed PVEH allows it to be conveniently matched with the environment by controlling the height of the liquid without a refabrication of the PVEH; this is difficult to achieve by most traditional resonant-type PVEHs. The results above confirmed the advantage of the PVEH using liquid as an energy-capturing medium to achieve ultralow frequency energy. Furthermore, it is noteworthy that the RMS value of the output power $( P _ { R M S } )$ of the proposed PVEH reached the level of microwatts $( 9 . 8 \mu \mathrm { W } )$ , whereas the vibration intensity applied to the proposed PVEH was only $0 . 0 3 { \mathrm { g } } ,$ which was much lower than the acceleration required by most PVEHs $_ { ( > 0 . 1 \mathrm { g } ) }$ to reach the same level. In addition, even if the vibration intensity is reduced to $_ { 0 . 0 2 \mathrm { g } } ,$ the maximum $P _ { R M S }$ of the proposed PVEH can still reach $3 . 9 7 \mu \mathrm { W }$ under an optimized resistance of $1 3 5 \mathrm { k } \Omega ,$ as shown in Fig. 4. Hence, the proposed PVEH has a low potential barrier and can easily harvest energy from lowintensity-vibration ambient environments. Moreover, the advantages of the proposed PVEH in terms of normalized energy density at low frequencies compared with those of various PVEHs are shown in Table II. ![](images/575b5b30aaf04845342248d645257b6ae64f832a0d5ee9a8d6db0fc4749fe8db.jpg) FIG. 6. Angle response of the PVEH with the acceleration of $0 . 0 3 { \mathfrak { g } }$ (a) P-1; (b) P-2; (c) P-3. Angle bandwidth of the PVEH: (d) P-1; (e) P-2; (f) P-3. Finally, to demonstrate the multidirectional characteristics of the PVEH, we herein propose three PVEHs with different numbers of floater-levers to ensure the same coverage range in the horizontal plane, as shown in Figs. 5(a)–5(c), where PVEH-1 (P-1) is composed of two fan-shaped floater-levers with a fan angle of $1 5 0 ^ { \circ }$ ; PVEH-2 (P-2), three fan-shaped floater-levers with a fan angle of $1 0 0 ^ { \circ }$ ; and PVEH-3 (P-3), four fan-shaped floater-levers with a fan angle of $7 5 ^ { \circ }$ . The total coverage angle range was $3 0 0 ^ { \circ }$ , whereas the remaining $ { } ^ { 6 0 ^ { \circ } }$ afforded sufficient movement space for the floater-levers such that they are not in contact with each other. In addition, the multidirectional vibration excitation in the horizontal plane is embodied by the angle c between the vibration direction and the y-axis set on the array of floater-levers, which are also depicted in Figs. $5 ( \mathrm { a } ) \mathrm { - } 5 ( \mathrm { c } )$ . Figures $6 ( \mathrm { a } ) \mathrm { - } 6 ( \mathrm { c } )$ show the angle responses of the output powers of P-1, P-2, and P-3 as functions of the vibration angle c at resonance frequencies of 3, 2.8, and $2 . 6 \mathrm { H z }$ , respectively. P-1 indicated a poor angle response and almost no output while the vibration direction reached $9 0 ^ { \circ }$ , as shown in Figs. 6(a) and $6 ( \mathrm { d } )$ . However, the angle responses of P-2 and P-3 were favorable, and their maximum output power deviations were approximately $2 4 . 9 2 \%$ and $2 8 . 3 1 \%$ , respectively, under vibrations in different directions. Consequently, an excellent angle response can be achieved by the PVEH if the numbers and sizes of the floater-levers are set reasonably. When the angle bandwidth30 (the range of angle c corresponding to the output of thep $\mathrm { P V E H } > \sqrt { 2 } / 2 \mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ or $1 / 2 \mathrm { P } _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ ) was used to evaluate the performance of the PVEH under a multidirectional vibration excitation, the angle bandwidths of the proposed P-2 and P-3 both reached $3 6 0 ^ { \circ }$ in the horizontal plane, as shown in Figs. $6 ( \mathrm { e } ) { - } 6 ( \mathrm { f } )$ . Even when using a higher standard of ${ \sqrt { 2 } } / { 2 \mathrm { P } _ { \mathrm { m a x } } } ,$ the angle bandwidths of the proposed P-2 and P-3 can still be maintained at $3 6 0 ^ { \circ }$ . In addition, the angle response of P-3 at different accelerations is shown in Fig. 7. The angle bandwidth of P-3 at different accelerations remained at $3 6 0 ^ { \circ }$ when $1 / 2 \mathrm { ~ P _ { m a x } }$ was used as the evaluation standard, which implies that the proposed PVEH can maintain a good angle response even at low vibration intensities. Table III shows that the angle response of the proposed PVEH with a single piezoelectric element was much better than those of most PVEHs with multiple piezoelectric elements. In addition, PVEHs with multiple piezoelectric elements require a complicated management circuit because of the phase difference between each piezoelectric element;28 however, we only used a single piezoelectric element, which simplified the design of the management circuit significantly. Additionally, we achieved ultralow frequency and low intensity vibration energy harvesting simultaneously, which is difficult to achieve by most PVEHs, as mentioned previously. Therefore, the proposed PVEH using liquid as an energy-capturing medium exhibits promising potential for applications. ![](images/4bfbfa4d7edf64b7e4d2e51a3087a224c009273708a3b38d9d833a431a663e93.jpg) FIG. 7. Angle response of the P-3 under different accelerations. It is noteworthy that the main purpose of this study is to demonstrate the advantages of the proposed PVEH under ultralow frequency, low intensity, and multidirectional vibrations, where the multidirectional vibrations are in the horizontal plane. However, for better evaluating the proposed PVEH, the performances of the proposed PVEH under the vibrations with a high acceleration and more directions in a vertical plane should also be investigated. Furthermore, issues such as the liquid evaporation, waterproof treatment of electronic components, and PZT beams must be considered; these will be addressed in our future studies. In summary, we proposed a PVEH using liquid as an energycapturing medium that can simultaneously achieve ultralow frequency, low-intensity, and multidirectional vibration energy harvesting in a horizontal plane. The PVEH with one floater-lever can generate a $P _ { R M S }$ of $9 . 8 \mu \mathrm { W }$ under an ultralow frequency $( 2 . 6 \mathrm { H z } )$ and a low intensity vibration excitation $\left( 0 . 0 3 { \mathrm { g } } \right)$ ; furthermore, its normalized energy density was $8 . 8 9 \mu \mathrm { W } / ( \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } \mathrm { g } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { \bar { H } z ) }$ , indicating its favorable ultralow frequency and low intensity characteristics. Moreover, the PVEH can easily adapt to the different ultralow frequency environments by changing the height of the liquid without the need for device refabrication. In addition, the PVEH with three and four floater-levers demonstrated excellent angle responses under multidirectional vibration excitations in the horizontal plane with frequencies below $3 \mathrm { H z }$ and an acceleration of $0 . 0 3 { \mathrm { g } } ,$ as demonstrated by the maximum output power deviations of $2 4 . 9 2 \%$ and $2 8 . 3 1 \%$ , respectively, under different vibration angles $\gamma$ $( 0 ^ { \circ } - 3 6 0 ^ { \circ } )$ ); furthermore, the angle bandwidths of both floater-levers reached $3 6 0 ^ { \circ }$ (using $\sqrt { 2 } / 2 \mathrm { P } _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ as the standard). All the experimental results demonstrated the potential of the proposed PVEH as an energy supply of WSNs distributed in ultralow frequency, low intensity, and multidirectional applications.
